cases.statement: Two carriers in one paper: Patient 2 (mosaic, detected in buccal DNA only), and a second suspected AxD patient tested by GeneDx, mentioned in one sentence with no clinical information.

people.label: Patient 2
people.zygosity_or_genotype: mosaic (heterozygous in buccal DNA, apparently in 100% of buccal cells; not detected in blood or nail DNA)
people.key_phenotypes: macrocephaly at birth (both parents with large heads); developmental delay and intermittent ataxia at 1 year; tonic-clonic seizures from 4 years 9 months; slight dysarthria and clumsy gait; MRI essentially normal apart from ventriculomegaly

quotes.quote: Buccal DNA of Patient 2 was analyzed for GFAP mutations by GeneDx (Gaithersburg, MD) due to several clinical signs consistent with AxD (macrocephaly, delayed development, clumsy gait, dysarthria, seizures) and negative tests for multiple other disorders.
In contrast, the relative peak heights for the mutant and wild type nucleotides in the buccal DNA sequence suggest that 100% of these cells carry the mutation (Fig. 4).
Nevertheless, the mutant allele remained undetectable in the patient blood DNA sample.
Thus Patient 2 appears to be an ectodermal mosaic for the GFAP mutation.
Patient 2 was macrocephalic at birth (98%), but his father’s head circumference was 61 cms (well above the 98%) and his mother’s was 57.5 cm (just below the 98%).
At 1 year of age he was evaluated for developmental delay and intermittent ataxia.
He was seizure free until 4 years 9 months, when he manifested tonic clonic seizures and staring episodes that were controlled with valproic acid.
At the age of 6 yrs and 7 months he had slight dysarthria and gait was slightly clumsy.
Subsequent MRIs at 3, 5 and 6 years of age were normal except for the ventriculomegaly and a small, stable T1 and T2 hypoenhancing region in the middle of the pituitary, thought unrelated to AxD.

people.label: unnamed person 1
people.key_phenotypes: not reported (described only as a suspected AxD patient; no clinical information)

quotes.quote: Another is that the patient has a disorder other than AxD, although AxD seems the simplest explanation given the presence of a de novo GFAP mutation, and that the same mutation was found by GeneDx for another suspected AxD patient (no clinical information is available for that patient; Sherri Bale, GeneDx, personal communication).

phenotype_specificity.statement: Clinical signs prompted GFAP testing after negative tests for multiple other disorders. MRI met none of the five AxD imaging criteria; the authors raise the possibility of a different disorder. Macrocephaly may be familial (both parents have large heads).

quotes.quote: Buccal DNA of Patient 2 was analyzed for GFAP mutations by GeneDx (Gaithersburg, MD) due to several clinical signs consistent with AxD (macrocephaly, delayed development, clumsy gait, dysarthria, seizures) and negative tests for multiple other disorders.
Patient 2 presented in infancy, yet meets none of these criteria.
Possible explanations include the nature of the mutation or its limited presence in the CNS due to mosaicism.
Patient 2 was macrocephalic at birth (98%), but his father’s head circumference was 61 cms (well above the 98%) and his mother’s was 57.5 cm (just below the 98%).

segregation.statement: Both parents' blood DNA was wild type. No other relatives reported.

quotes.quote: Surprisingly, the blood DNAs from both the parents and the patient proved to be wild type.

de_novo.statement: Both parents tested (blood DNA) and lacked the variant; the variant is mosaic in the patient (buccal positive, blood and nails negative). A marker panel 'used for paternity testing' was used to confirm that the patient's blood and buccal samples came from the same individual; confirmation of parentage itself is not stated.

quotes.quote: Surprisingly, the blood DNAs from both the parents and the patient proved to be wild type.
The possibility of a sample mix-up was eliminated by DNA analysis by the UAB Medical Genomics Lab using a panel of markers used for paternity testing.
These tests documented that the two DNA samples came from the same individual.
Since the I/D/F mutation in Patient 2 is mosaic, it clearly arose de novo (as expected, it was not found in the blood DNA of either parent).

functional.statement: Construct assay in transiently transfected SW13vim- cells (not patient cells): the mutant formed thick, mainly perinuclear bundles instead of the fine network of wild type; a 1:1 co-transfection with wild type gave the mutant pattern.

quotes.quote: The mutant protein did assemble into filaments, but unlike the fine filamentous network that coursed throughout the cell that is typically produced by wild type GFAP (Fig. 2A), the I/D/F mutant GFAP consistently produced thick bundles that were primarily perinuclear (Fig. 2E).

Co-transfection of a 1:1 mixture of mutant and wild type expression vectors produced an assembly pattern identical to that of the mutant alone, except for a general increase in diffuse background staining (data not shown).

variant_type_and_mechanism.statement: Deletion-insertion causing a frameshift at the extreme C-terminus, p.(Val431AspfsTer14): changes the last two amino acids and extends the protein by 11 residues (no premature stop). Authors liken its effect to an insertion and describe dominance over wild type.

quotes.quote: This is predicted to alter the identity of the last two amino acids of the wild type protein and to elongate the tail by an additional 11 amino acids (p.Val431Aspfs*14) (Fig. 4).
Although this mutation technically produces a frameshift, its effect is essentially the same as an insertion since it occurs at the very end of the protein.
This is consistent with the dominant nature of the heterozygous GFAP mutations associated with AxD.

authors_classification.statement: Authors call it disease-causing; no ACMG criteria stated.

quotes.quote: This provides very strong evidence that the mutation is disease causing.

concerns: Mosaic finding: present in buccal DNA, absent from blood (allele-specific PCR sensitive to 1 in 1,000) and from nail DNA.
Transcript: the paper uses NM_002055.4, not NM_002055.5.
The second carrier (GeneDx, personal communication) has no clinical information and no label; whether it is a distinct person is taken from the authors' word 'another'.
MRI essentially normal, which the authors note is unusual for infantile AxD; the authors raise an alternative diagnosis.
Macrocephaly may be familial: both parents' head circumferences are at or above the 98th percentile.
notes_for_panel: Strong de novo evidence (both parents negative, mosaic in the child) and a construct assay. Phenotype is mild and atypical, with normal MRI.
